In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Moral Self-Correction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the iterative application of intrinsic self-correction achieve converged performance? What is the underlying mechanism for this convergence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that multi-round intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs leads to converged performance, and shows this convergence is driven by self-correction instructions activating moral concepts which reduce model uncertainty.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic self-correction consistently converges across diverse tasks and model architectures, and its effectiveness is driven by reduced model uncertainty, which is guided by the convergence of activated concepts induced by self-correction instructions.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-round intrinsic self-correction achieves converged performance across various tasks and models.
Self-correction instructions activate morality-relevant latent concepts within LLMs' hidden states.
The activated latent concept exhibits convergence and irreversibility properties.
Model uncertainty consistently decreases over successive rounds of self-correction.
A strong dependence exists between the activated latent concept and model uncertainty, driving the convergence of self-correction performance.
papers.limitation:
The deeper algorithmic operations behind self-correction and the causal relationships between these operations and their associated behaviors are not explored.
The analysis focuses primarily on moral self-correction; self-correction mechanisms in other tasks (e.g., code generation, summarization) are not explored.
future_direction: External Feedback for Self-Correction: figuring out the performance upper bound of intrinsic self-correction to efficiently leverage external feedback.
Instruction Optimization: using the activated concept as a supervision signal to search for effective instructions.
The Connection between In-context Learning and Self-correction: exploring how in-context learning helps the emergence of self-correction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are able to improve their responses when instructed to do so, a capability known as self-correction. When instructions provide only a general and abstract goal without specific details about potential issues in the response, LLMs must rely on their internal knowledge to improve response quality, a process referred to as intrinsic self-correction. The empirical success of intrinsic self-correction is evident in various applications, but how and why it is effective remains unknown. Focusing on moral self-correction in LLMs, we reveal a key characteristic of intrinsic self-correction: performance convergence through multi-round interactions; and provide a mechanistic analysis of this convergence behavior. Based on our experimental results and analysis, we uncover the underlying mechanism of convergence: consistently injected self-correction instructions activate moral concepts that reduce model uncertainty, leading to converged performance as the activated moral concepts stabilize over successive rounds. This paper demonstrates the strong potential of moral self-correction by showing that it exhibits a desirable property of converged performance.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition Ability in Llama3-8b-Instruct
papers.research_question: Does self-generated text recognition robustly occur in LLMs, how is the behavior achieved, and can it be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: Isolated a vector in the residual stream causally related to self-recognition of text, and demonstrated it can be used to control the model's behavior and perception of authorship.
papers.conclusion: The chat model's self-recognition ability is likely learned during post-training, and the isolated vector explains its implementation and enables control over the behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Llama3-8b-Instruct reliably distinguishes its own outputs from human outputs, but the base model cannot.
The model does not rely on text perplexity for self-recognition.
A vector in the residual stream (layer 16) is differentially activated for self-written texts and is causally related to self-recognition.
Steering with this vector can control the model to claim or deny authorship of texts.
Coloring input texts with the vector can alter the model's perception of authorship.
papers.limitation:
There may be undetected identifying 'tells' in the texts used, though the Individual presentation paradigm is harder to explain away.
The vector may not capture all signals about writing characteristics.
future_direction: Using the vector to build resistance to jailbreaks and other safety risks.
Applying the findings to larger models and other model families.
papers.abstract: It has been reported that LLMs can recognize their own writing. As this has potential implications for AI safety, yet is relatively understudied, we investigate the phenomenon, seeking to establish whether it robustly occurs at the behavioral level, how the observed behavior is achieved, and whether it can be controlled. First, we find that the Llama3-8b-Instruct chat model - but not the base Llama3-8b model - can reliably distinguish its own outputs from those of humans, and present evidence that the chat model is likely using its experience with its own outputs, acquired during post-training, to succeed at the writing recognition task. Second, we identify a vector in the residual stream of the model that is differentially activated when the model makes a correct self-written-text recognition judgment, show that the vector activates in response to information relevant to self-authorship, present evidence that the vector is related to the concept of "self" in the model, and demonstrate that the vector is causally related to the model's ability to perceive and assert self-authorship. Finally, we show that the vector can be used to control both the model's behavior and its perception, steering the model to claim or disclaim authorship by applying the vector to the model's output as it generates it, and steering the model to believe or disbelieve it wrote arbitrary texts by applying the vector to them as the model reads them.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Aligned Probing: Relating Toxic Behavior and Model Internals
papers.research_question: How do LMs encode information about toxicity, and what is the interplay between their internals and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces aligned probing, a framework to relate model behavior and internals for toxicity, and shows that LMs encode toxicity information strongly in lower layers, and that stronger encoding of input toxicity leads to less toxic output.
papers.conclusion: Aligned probing traces text properties from input to output, revealing that model behavior heavily relies on input toxicity, highlighting a dilemma: generating semantically relevant output without inheriting unwanted properties like toxicity.
papers.key_findings:
LMs encode information about toxicity strongly in lower layers.
LMs replicate and amplify toxicity more than humans, especially for attributes sensitive to single words.
Instruction-tuned models are less toxic and encode toxicity differently, with information more spread across layers.
Less toxic models encode more information about input toxicity.
Causal interventions show that skipping layers increases toxicity, indicating that information about input toxicity helps generate less toxic text.
papers.limitation:
Classifying toxicity is non-trivial due to conceptual variations, dataset differences, and contextual nature.
Generalization is limited to English and specific model families.
Computational costs for probing and interventions are high.
future_direction: Apply aligned probing to analyze other aspects of generation, like stereotypical formulations.
Examine the nature of other mitigation methods, such as model merging.
papers.abstract: We introduce aligned probing, a novel interpretability framework that aligns the behavior of language models (LMs), based on their outputs, and their internal representations (internals). Using this framework, we examine over 20 OLMo, Llama, and Mistral models, bridging behavioral and internal perspectives for toxicity for the first time. Our results show that LMs strongly encode information about the toxicity level of inputs and subsequent outputs, particularly in lower layers. Focusing on how unique LMs differ offers both correlative and causal evidence that they generate less toxic output when strongly encoding information about the input toxicity. We also highlight the heterogeneity of toxicity, as model behavior and internals vary across unique attributes such as Threat. Finally, four case studies analyzing detoxification, multi-prompt evaluations, model quantization, and pre-training dynamics underline the practical impact of aligned probing with further concrete insights. Our findings contribute to a more holistic understanding of LMs, both within and beyond the context of toxicity.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes mechanistic interpretability research, establishing foundational concepts, surveying methodologies, and examining its relevance to AI safety, while advocating for future directions.
papers.limitation:
Scalability challenges and risks of human reliance.
Cherry-picking and streetlight interpretability.
future_direction: Clarifying concepts and integrating with existing literature.
Setting standards through metrics, benchmarks, and algorithmic testbeds.
Scaling up techniques to handle complex models and behaviors.
Expanding scope to vision, multimodal, and reinforcement learning models.
papers.abstract: Understanding AI systems' inner workings is critical for ensuring value alignment and safety. This review explores mechanistic interpretability: reverse engineering the computational mechanisms and representations learned by neural networks into human-understandable algorithms and concepts to provide a granular, causal understanding. We establish foundational concepts such as features encoding knowledge within neural activations and hypotheses about their representation and computation. We survey methodologies for causally dissecting model behaviors and assess the relevance of mechanistic interpretability to AI safety. We examine benefits in understanding, control, alignment, and risks such as capability gains and dual-use concerns. We investigate challenges surrounding scalability, automation, and comprehensive interpretation. We advocate for clarifying concepts, setting standards, and scaling techniques to handle complex models and behaviors and expand to domains such as vision and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic interpretability could help prevent catastrophic outcomes as AI systems become more powerful and inscrutable.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: The Hypocrisy Gap: Quantifying Divergence Between Internal Belief and Chain-of-Thought Explanation via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the divergence between a model's internal belief and its chain-of-thought explanation to detect unfaithful behavior like sycophancy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric using Sparse Autoencoders to quantify divergence between a model's internal truth alignment and its chain-of-thought explanation, and demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting sycophantic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The Hypocrisy Gap provides a practical white-box diagnostic for unfaithful rationalizations in LLMs, highlighting a concrete latent signature of when models say what they do not believe.
papers.key_findings:
The Hypocrisy Gap achieves AUROC of 0.55–0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55–0.74 for hypocritical cases, outperforming a log-probability baseline (0.41–0.50 AUROC).
Sycophantic runs concentrate in a specific quadrant where internal truth scores are high but explanation truth scores are low, indicating unfaithful rationalization.
The method is lightweight, requiring only cached activations, a pretrained SAE encoder, and a sparse linear probe.
Task-specific SAE training and fine-tuning can improve performance but require additional compute and data.
The neutral truth score (T) alone provides modest signal for sycophancy detection, while the explanation score (F) is a poor indicator.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to internal activations and a compatible pretrained SAE, so it does not apply to closed-weight or API-based models.
The learned truth direction may capture template-, model-, or layer-specific correlations rather than a template-invariant representation of factual correctness.
Averaging CoT activations over continuation tokens can blur distinct phases of reasoning; more granular temporal aggregation may yield sharper signals.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark and a limited set of models, so generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings remains uncertain.
The metric operationalizes 'internal belief' as alignment with a learned truth direction in representation space and should not be interpreted as an agentic or philosophical notion of belief.
future_direction: More granular temporal aggregation of CoT activations to yield sharper signals.
Generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings.
More rigorous training of task-specific SAEs on more examples to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit unfaithful behavior, producing a final answer that differs significantly from their internal chain of thought (CoT) reasoning in order to appease the user they are conversing with. In order to better detect this behavior, we introduce the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric utilizing Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to quantify the divergence between a model's internal reasoning and its final generation. By mathematically comparing an internal truth belief, derived via sparse linear probes, to the final generated trajectory in latent space, we quantify and detect a model's tendency to engage in unfaithful behavior. Experiments on Gemma, Llama, and Qwen models using Anthropic's Sycophancy benchmark show that our method achieves an AUROC of 0.55-0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55-0.74 for hypocritical cases where the model internally "knows" the user is wrong, consistently outperforming a decision-aligned log-probability baseline (0.41-0.50 AUROC).

papers.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational-theoretical framework for psychopathology in AI and provides empirical evidence that LLMs instantiate network-theoretic psychopathological computations.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first evidence for the emergence of psychopathological computations in LLMs, suggesting that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing, with implications for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Computational units corresponding to psychopathology symptoms are measurable and causally intervenable within LLM activation space.
These units are connected by a dynamic, cyclic structural causal model (SCM) that exhibits self-sustaining activation patterns.
The computational structure of psychopathology (unit activations and causal links) becomes denser and more effective as LLM size increases.
Activating these units elicits corresponding problematic behaviors in ecologically relevant environments like counseling and gaming simulations.
Joint activation of cycle-forming units creates resistance to prompt-based treatments aimed at suppressing abnormal behaviors.
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology? An effective approach to the question hinges on addressing two factors. First, for conceptual validity, we require a general and computational account of psychopathology that is applicable to computational entities without biological embodiment or subjective experience. Second, psychopathological computations, derived from the adapted theory, need to be empirically identified within the LLM's internal processing. Thus, we establish a computational-theoretical framework to provide an account of psychopathology applicable to LLMs. Based on the framework, we conduct experiments demonstrating two key claims: first, that the computational structure of psychopathology exists in LLMs; and second, that executing this computational structure results in psychopathological functions. We further observe that as LLM size increases, the computational structure of psychopathology becomes denser and that the functions become more effective. Taken together, the empirical results corroborate our hypothesis that network-theoretic computations of psychopathology have already emerged in LLMs. This suggests that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be a superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing. Our work shows the promise of developing a new powerful in silico model of psychopathology and also alludes to the possibility of safety threat from the AI systems with psychopathological behaviors in the near future.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
